topic: Part IV Scientific Computing: exact Fourier resource theorem versus QPE certificate
question: The chapter 'Fourier transforms, phase estimation and amplitude estimation' (part-iv-quantum-scientific-computing:qsc-fourier-estimation) is linked to cluster oai-exact-fourier, which the curriculum describes as a route to 'Use the Comparator-backed exact Fourier route as an external resource theorem after circuit-model adaptation; it does not itself certify QPE.' Explain precisely why possessing a comparator-backed exact-Fourier circuit construction does NOT constitute a certificate for quantum phase estimation, and enumerate the additional resource and correctness obligations that QPE requires beyond the Fourier primitive. Do not assert the exact phase-estimation theorem or its error bound from the primary notes.
reference_answer: An exact-Fourier circuit construction is a single primitive: it realizes the quantum Fourier transform with some gate set and resource tuple. The intake records oai-exact-fourier as a 'source-route' with next_action 'compare circuit ordering, gate set and cost tuple with the local circuit/resource API; do not present the Fourier result as a block encoding or QPE certificate.' QPE is a composite algorithm that consumes the QFT but additionally requires: (1) controlled applications of the target unitary U (or its powers U^{2^k}), i.e. an access/oracle model whose construction cost must be charged separately; (2) an eigenstate or input-state preparation assumption and the overlap of the input with eigenvectors, which governs success probability; (3) an approximation/precision analysis relating the number of ancilla phase qubits to the estimated-phase resolution and failure probability; (4) readout/measurement of the phase register and the classical post-processing, which the AGENT_GOAL's resource track insists be charged; and (5) a circuit-model adaptation reconciling the Fourier route's qubit/gate ordering with the local circuit and resource API. None of these are supplied by the Fourier primitive alone, so comparator-backed Fourier status certifies only the transform, not the end-to-end QPE claim. The correct status is a conditional resource-decomposition question; the exact QPE error bound stays unscored pending a read primary-source anchor.

topic: Part III Quantum Information: pure states as rank-one projectors satisfying the density-operator axioms
question: Let H = C^d with the standard inner product of Eq. (2.4), and let |psi> in H be a unit vector, <psi|psi> = 1. Define rho := |psi><psi|. Starting only from Definition 2.1 (a quantum state is a density operator with rho >= 0 and tr rho = 1), prove that rho is a legitimate quantum state, that it is a rank-one orthogonal projector (rho^2 = rho = rho^dagger), and explain in what precise sense this makes rho an extreme point (pure state) of the convex set of density operators. State explicitly which step uses normalization of |psi> and why dropping it breaks the trace condition.
reference_answer: Hermiticity: rho^dagger = (|psi><psi|)^dagger = |psi><psi| = rho. Positivity: for any |phi>, <phi|rho|phi> = <phi|psi><psi|phi> = |<psi|phi>|^2 >= 0, hence rho >= 0. Trace/normalization: in any orthonormal basis, tr rho = sum_i <e_i|psi><psi|e_i> = <psi|(sum_i |e_i><e_i|)|psi> = <psi|psi> = 1, where the final equality is exactly the unit-norm hypothesis computed with the Eq. (2.4) inner product. Both Definition 2.1 conditions hold, so rho is a quantum state. Idempotency: rho^2 = |psi><psi|psi><psi| = <psi|psi>|psi><psi| = rho, so rho is an orthogonal projector onto the one-dimensional span{|psi>}, hence rank 1. Extreme point: if rho = p sigma_1 + (1-p) sigma_2 with 0<p<1 and density operators sigma_i, positivity forces the range of each sigma_i inside range(rho) = span{|psi>}; the only trace-one state supported on a one-dimensional space is |psi><psi|, so sigma_1 = sigma_2 = rho and the decomposition is trivial. Thus rho is an extreme point (pure state), matching the text's statement that a pure density matrix has rank 1 and equals a projector |psi><psi|. If normalization were dropped (<psi|psi> = c != 1) then tr rho = c != 1 violates Definition 2.1, and (|psi><psi|)^2 = c|psi><psi| != rho, so one must renormalize rho = |psi><psi|/<psi|psi> to recover a state.

topic: Part III Quantum Information: partial trace of the Bell state gives a maximally mixed marginal
question: Consider the two-qubit EPR/Bell state |Phi+>_AB = (1/sqrt 2)(|0>_A|0>_B + |1>_A|1>_B) with density matrix Phi+_AB = |Phi+><Phi+| as in Eqs. (2.17)-(2.18). Using the defining relation Eq. (2.14), tr(rho_AB (X_A tensor 1_B)) = tr(rho_A X_A) for all X_A, and/or the basis formula Eq. (2.15), compute the marginal rho_A = tr_B Phi+_AB and show rho_A = (1/2) 1 (Eq. (2.22)). Explain why this maximally mixed marginal shows Phi+ is not a product state, and why the partial trace is independent of the orthonormal basis chosen in Eq. (2.15).
reference_answer: Write |Phi+> = (1/sqrt2) sum_{i in {0,1}} |i>_A|i>_B. Using Eq. (2.15) with the computational B-basis: tr_B Phi+_AB = sum_k (1_A tensor <k|_B) |Phi+><Phi+| (1_A tensor |k>_B). Since (1_A tensor <k|_B)|Phi+> = (1/sqrt2)|k>_A, each term is (1/2)|k>_A<k|_A, and summing over k in {0,1} gives rho_A = (1/2)(|0><0| + |1><1|) = (1/2)1, the maximally mixed state (Eq. 2.22). Equivalently via Eq. (2.14): tr(Phi+_AB (X_A tensor 1_B)) = (1/2)(<0|X_A|0> + <1|X_A|1>) = (1/2) tr X_A = tr((1/2)1 X_A) for all X_A, so by uniqueness rho_A = (1/2)1. Not a product state: a pure global state has a pure marginal iff it is a product; here rho_A = (1/2)1 is maximally mixed (eigenvalues 1/2,1/2, rank 2), so if Phi+ = omega_A tensor sigma_B its A-marginal would be the pure omega_A, contradicting rho_A = (1/2)1. A pure global state with a mixed marginal is by definition entangled. Basis independence: Eq. (2.14) defines rho_A uniquely by its action against all X_A with no reference to a basis; Eq. (2.15) merely evaluates that unique operator, so every orthonormal {|e_i>_B} yields the same rho_A, as the text explicitly notes.

topic: Part IV Scientific Computing: additive error of an LCU sum of block encodings (Proposition 9.10)
question: Proposition 9.10 (Lin-Wiebe, p.149) states that given block encodings U_{A_j} in BE_{alpha_j,a}(A_j, eps_j), j in [M], M=2^m, alpha_j >= 0, with select oracle U_SEL = sum_j |j><j| tensor U_{A_j} and prepare oracle V_PREP|0^m> = (1/sqrt gamma) sum_j sqrt(alpha_j)|j>, gamma = sum_j alpha_j, the operator W = (V_PREP^dagger tensor I) U_SEL (V_PREP tensor I) satisfies W in BE_{gamma, a+m}(sum_j A_j, sum_j eps_j). Derive (i) the subnormalization factor of the sum and (ii) the total block-encoding error, prove the error bound, and explain why the errors add (not the max) and why gamma = sum_j alpha_j rather than something smaller.
reference_answer: Set B_j := <0^a|U_{A_j}|0^a>, so by BE_{alpha_j,a}(A_j,eps_j) we have ||A_j - alpha_j B_j|| <= eps_j and ||B_j|| <= 1. Computing the (|0^m,0^a>) block of W, the prepare amplitudes sqrt(alpha_j)/sqrt(gamma) on each side contract through U_SEL to weight term j by (sqrt(alpha_j)/sqrt(gamma))^2 = alpha_j/gamma, giving <0^m,0^a|W|0^m,0^a> = sum_j (alpha_j/gamma) B_j (Eq. 9.41). (i) Hence W encodes gamma * sum_j (alpha_j/gamma) B_j with subnormalization gamma = sum_j alpha_j and target sum_j A_j. (ii) The error is ||sum_j A_j - gamma<0^m,0^a|W|0^m,0^a>|| = ||sum_j (A_j - alpha_j B_j)|| <= sum_j ||A_j - alpha_j B_j|| <= sum_j eps_j by the triangle inequality (Eq. 9.42), so W in BE_{gamma,a+m}(sum_j A_j, sum_j eps_j). Errors add because each term independently contributes its deviation A_j - alpha_j B_j and the triangle inequality admits no cancellation guarantee, so sum_j eps_j (not the max) is the faithful worst-case bound. gamma = sum_j alpha_j is forced by unit-norm of the prepare state: |V_PREP|0^m>|^2 = (1/gamma) sum_j alpha_j = 1; any smaller gamma makes the amplitudes exceed norm one and V_PREP non-unitary. The a+m ancilla count is the a block ancillas plus the m-qubit control register indexing the M = 2^m summands.

rubric.criterion: Identifies B_j = <0^a|U_{A_j}|0^a> with ||A_j-alpha_j B_j||<=eps_j, ||B_j||<=1, and computes the W block = sum_j (alpha_j/gamma)B_j

Proves total error <= sum_j eps_j via the triangle inequality and explains why errors add not max
Justifies gamma = sum_j alpha_j by unit-norm of V_PREP|0^m> and notes a+m ancilla accounting

topic: Part IV Scientific Computing: multiplicative error of a product of block encodings on disjoint ancillas (Proposition 9.12)
question: Proposition 9.12 (Lin-Wiebe, p.150) block-encodes a product A_{M-1}...A_0 by applying U_{A_j} in BE_{alpha_j, a_j}(A_j, eps_j) sequentially on disjoint ancilla registers and a common system register, yielding U in BE_{prod_j alpha_j, sum_j a_j}(A_{M-1}...A_0, prod_j (alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_j alpha_j). Prove the error bound by induction on M, using ||B_j|| <= 1 and ||A_j|| <= alpha_j+eps_j. Then contrast this multiplicative error growth with the additive error of the sum construction (Prop. 9.10) and explain the resource meaning of disjoint ancilla registers.
reference_answer: For each j set B_j := <0^{a_j}|U_{A_j}|0^{a_j}>, so ||A_j - alpha_j B_j|| <= eps_j, ||B_j|| <= 1, and ||A_j|| <= ||A_j - alpha_j B_j|| + alpha_j||B_j|| <= alpha_j+eps_j. Disjoint ancillas make the all-zero ancilla block factorize: <0^{a_0+...+a_{M-1}}|U|0^{...}> = B_{M-1}...B_0 (Eq. 9.45). We prove ||prod_j A_j - prod_j (alpha_j B_j)|| <= prod_j(alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_j alpha_j by induction on M. Base M=1: ||A_0 - alpha_0 B_0|| <= eps_0 = (alpha_0+eps_0) - alpha_0. Step: let P = prod_{j<=M-2}A_j, P~ = prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j B_j). Then ||A_{M-1}P - (alpha_{M-1}B_{M-1})P~|| <= ||(A_{M-1}-alpha_{M-1}B_{M-1})P|| + ||alpha_{M-1}B_{M-1}(P-P~)|| <= eps_{M-1}||P|| + alpha_{M-1}||P-P~||. With ||P|| <= prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) and the induction hypothesis ||P-P~|| <= prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_{j<=M-2}alpha_j, this is <= eps_{M-1}prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) + alpha_{M-1}[prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_{j<=M-2}alpha_j] = (alpha_{M-1}+eps_{M-1})prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) - alpha_{M-1}prod_{j<=M-2}alpha_j = prod_j(alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_j alpha_j, completing the induction. Contrast: the sum (Prop. 9.10) has additive error sum_j eps_j and additive subnormalization gamma=sum_j alpha_j; the product has multiplicative subnormalization prod_j alpha_j and error prod(alpha_j+eps_j)-prod alpha_j, which for small eps_j is approximately (prod alpha_j) sum_j (eps_j/alpha_j) -- relative errors add while absolute error is amplified by the product of subnormalizations. Disjoint ancilla registers: each factor keeps its own a_j ancillas (not reused), so total ancilla cost is sum_j a_j; disjointness is exactly what lets the zero-ancilla block factor into B_{M-1}...B_0. This is simple but not ancilla-optimal (the text notes Example 11.9/Fig. 9.6 reduces a two-factor product to a+1 ancillas via deferred measurement).

assumptions: Each U_{A_j} is an (alpha_j, a_j, eps_j)-block encoding; registers a_0,...,a_{M-1} disjoint, system register shared.

conventions: BE_{alpha,a}(A,eps): ||A - alpha<0^a|U|0^a>|| <= eps, ||<0^a|U|0^a>|| <= 1.
